title: Concerto for Flute and Harp in C major
hook: Salon music for a duke who played the flute and his daughter, the harpist, written in Paris and never paid for.

painting.title: English Tea in the Salon des Quatre-Glaces at the Palais du Temple
painting.pairingNote: A Paris salon making music over tea, with the child Mozart at the keyboard: the aristocratic world the concerto was written for twelve years later.

facts: Mozart wrote it in Paris in April 1778, during his seven-month stay there. It was commissioned by the Duc de Guînes, an aristocrat and keen amateur flautist, for himself and his daughter Marie-Louise-Philippine, a harpist, who was taking composition lessons from Mozart.

In a letter to his father Mozart said the duke played the flute extremely well and the daughter the harp “magnifique”. As a composition pupil she disappointed him. The duke never paid for the concerto, and Mozart refused the half fee for the lessons offered through the housekeeper.
It is Mozart’s only concerto with a harp. In his day the harp was not yet a regular member of the orchestra, and pairing it with the flute was unusual.

In shape it is close to the [[sinfonia-concertante|sinfonia concertante]], a piece for several soloists that was then the fashion in Paris. Mozart left no cadenzas for it; those by the 19th-century composer Carl Reinecke are the most often played, as here.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a bright, courtly first movement (I), a slow song for strings and soloists (II), a dancing finale (III).

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: The orchestra opens with a bold, rising figure on the notes of C major, and sets out the themes before the soloists join. Then flute and harp take everything over, trading the melody and the accompaniment between them. It is a concerto movement in [[sonata-form|sonata form]], with a [[double-exposition|double exposition]] and a long cadenza for the two soloists together.

mainIdeas.name: The opening figure
mainIdeas.description: a loud, rising call on the notes of the home chord, then quick runs.

mainIdeas.name: The duet
mainIdeas.description: the flute singing a line while the harp ripples underneath in broken chords, and then the other way round.

stops.hear: The full orchestra, loud and bright: a rising call on the notes of a chord, then quick, busy runs
Flute and harp enter together with the opening call; the harp’s notes ripple underneath
The two take turns: one plays the tune, the other accompanies; the orchestra mostly listens
The orchestra alone, loud, for a few bars
stops.happening: The end of the soloists’ exposition

stops.hear: Flute and harp almost alone; the music wanders through new keys and grows tense with rising, sliding lines
The bold opening call in the orchestra again
The orchestra builds up and stops on a held chord
The orchestra is silent; flute and harp play alone, ending on a long trill

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The orchestra alone brings the movement to a bright close

notice: Listen to the harp when the flute has the tune. Its quick broken chords are the accompaniment a keyboard would usually play.
In the cadenza, notice how the two instruments imitate each other, one starting a phrase and the other finishing it.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The flautist Wolfgang Schulz and the Spanish harpist Nicanor Zabaleta recorded the concerto in the Musikverein in Vienna in May 1975, playing Reinecke’s cadenzas. On the Spotify album the concerto is tracks 4–6, after Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto with the same orchestra and conductor.

movements.heading: Andantino
movements.summary: A slow, songlike movement in F major. The strings set out short, gentle phrases, and the soloists answer and extend them into longer lines. The horns fall silent. Halfway through, the opening music comes back, and a quiet cadenza leads to a short close.

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: short, tender phrases in the strings, taken up by the flute.

mainIdeas.name: The harp’s ripple
mainIdeas.description: broken chords that keep the music moving.

stops.hear: Strings alone, soft and gentle, in short phrases
The flute and harp enter and spin the phrases into longer lines
For a moment the strings are alone again
The harp’s quick, rippling notes lead the way while the flute holds long notes
stops.happening: A link back to the opening

stops.hear: The gentle opening phrases return, with the soloists
The strings stop; flute and harp play alone, quietly

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: Strings and soloists together, very softly

notice: With the horns silent, the strings lead and the soloists answer. Notice how close and intimate it sounds after the first movement.

movements.heading: Rondeau: Allegro
movements.summary: A lively finale in the French manner: a *rondeau*, in which a dancing tune keeps coming back between new episodes. The orchestra plays it first, and at length. Then harp and flute enter, and much of the movement is a game of turns: one soloist plays while the other rests.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: a bright, graceful tune for the orchestra.

mainIdeas.name: The turns
mainIdeas.description: harp passages with the orchestra, then flute passages, then both together.

stops.hear: The orchestra alone plays a bright, dancing tune and its continuation
The harp enters; a few seconds later the flute joins
stops.happening: The soloists take up the tune

stops.hear: The flute stops; the harp plays on its own with the orchestra
Now the harp rests and the flute takes over
The orchestra alone again, with the dancing tune
Another short passage for the orchestra alone
stops.happening: The way to the last section

stops.hear: The orchestra stops; flute and harp alone

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Everyone together; the concerto ends with three loud C major chords

notice: Follow the soloists’ turns in the first half. Mozart gives each its own spell with the orchestra, as if letting father and daughter shine one at a time.

threads.title: Music for a salon
threads.body: Mozart wrote for two aristocratic amateurs and their guests, and the concerto keeps to elegant, well-mannered melody.

threads.title: A rare pair
threads.body: Flute and harp share the solo role equally; in the long cadenzas they finish each other’s phrases.

threads.title: Paris
threads.body: The *sinfonia concertante* shape and the *rondeau* finale, with its French name, both suit the city where it was written.
